scenario: A 52-year-old man starts hydralazine. His pressure falls and his heart rate rises from 70 to 110. He feels pounding. A classmate raises the hydralazine dose to treat the fast rate.
question: Why did the rate rise, and what should be added instead of more dilator?
options: More hydralazine for the fast rate
Reflex sympathetic drive. Add a beta blocker
A pure venous dilator, which causes the same reflex as hydralazine
A fluid bolus, because rate of 110 means hypovolemia from the first pill
A alpha blocker, which slows this reflex
correctAnswer: Reflex sympathetic drive. Add a beta blocker
explanation:
Hydralazine dilates arterioles. Baroreceptor reflex then raises heart rate, so it is paired with a beta blocker. The drop in pressure unloads the baroreceptors, so sympathetic tone speeds the heart. More dilator deepens the reflex. A beta blocker blunts it. Katzung BG, Vanderah TW. Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 15th ed. McGraw Hill; 2021.

Reflex sympathetic drive. Add a beta blocker
More hydralazine for the fast rate — More dilation speeds the heart further.
A pure venous dilator, which causes the same reflex as hydralazine — Venous dilators drop preload with less of this arterial reflex.
A fluid bolus, because rate of 110 means hypovolemia from the first pill — The rate is reflex, not volume loss.
A alpha blocker, which slows this reflex — Alpha blockade would dilate further. Beta blockade is the pair.
citation: Katzung BG, Vanderah TW. Basic and Clinical Pharmacology. 15th ed. McGraw Hill; 2021.
